new: The seller pays the commission from the proceeds. Chapter 3 sets out the two norms in use: on a EUR 28 million sale, about EUR 1.7 million under the MYBA sliding scale and EUR 2.8 million under the US flat 10 percent. Where another broker introduces the buyer, that broker is paid from the seller’s commission, typically half of it or a little less. Sellers do not always know which norm applies, so the scale and any split belong in the listing agreement. If the central agent also finds the buyer, it acts for both sides. new: The sale contract is usually the MYBA Memorandum of Agreement, described from the buyer’s side in chapter 4, and it binds the seller in the same terms. The buyer pays a deposit, typically 10 percent, on signing. The seller’s warranties are narrow. Andrew Charlier of HFW describes them as the right to sell and delivery free of mortgages, liens and other claims, with exclusion clauses ruling out any warranty on condition beyond what the agreement states. Liens are discharged before closing (BOAT International, September 2025). Under the 2021 MYBA E-MoA the seller also warrants that no undischarged tax or VAT liability has been incurred (Penningtons Manches Cooper, April 2022), so the evidence of the yacht’s VAT status should be ready before listing. The warranties are usually backed by a guarantee, in a form MYBA provides, from the beneficial owner or a company on its behalf; Ezio Dal Maso of Stephenson Harwood notes that its scope, cap and expiry are settled deal by deal (September 2026).

old: The 30 to 50 percent overrun is what the work actually costs against an initial scope built on imperfect information, not a project management failure. Maltby describes the overrun the same way, as partly a pricing problem and partly a contract problem. The first part is budgeted for; the second is contained.
